change_summary: Adds forwards against futures, options (with an importer call-option example) and interest rate swaps, with three questions. Exchange Rates and Forex Business is still only partly covered.

items.title: Reading a two-way quote
items.core_explanation_md:
A dealer rarely gives one price. A quote such as USD/INR 83.2450/83.2550 carries two: the rate at which the **quoting bank buys** a dollar (the bid, 83.2450) and the rate at which it **sells** one (the offer, 83.2550). Both sides are named from the bank's point of view, never the customer's.

India uses the direct method: one unit of foreign currency is priced in a varying number of rupees. Under a direct quote the bank buys low and sells high. So an exporter's dollars are bought on the bid side and an importer's dollars are sold on the offer side; for customers the bank then moves each side further in its own favour by an exchange margin. The rates here are illustrative.
items.expanded_explanation_md:
An indirect quote turns the picture round: the home currency is the fixed unit (for example ₹100) and the number of foreign currency units varies. In the international market the pound, the euro, the Australian dollar and the New Zealand dollar are quoted this way against the US dollar: one unit of that currency for so many dollars.

The dealer's rule turns round as well. With an indirect quote the bank quotes the lower figure when it sells, because handing over fewer foreign units for the same amount of home currency is the dearer price.

items.title: Two quotes for one import payment
items.core_explanation_md: A customer rate is the interbank rate moved in the bank's favour by an exchange margin. That lets you compare quotes that are worded differently. Illustrative case: an importer must pay USD 40,000 while interbank spot USD/INR is 83.4125/83.4175. Bank A says it will add a margin of 6 paise to the interbank rate. Bank B simply quotes an all-in rate of 83.4700. Which bank costs the importer less, and what margin is Bank B really charging?

worked_steps.description: The importer is buying dollars, so both banks are selling: the starting point is the interbank selling rate.
Bank A: add its margin, because a bank sells high.
Cost at Bank A.
Cost at Bank B at its all-in rate.
Margin hidden inside Bank B's rate.
Saving by choosing Bank B.

items.final_answer_with_unit: Bank B is cheaper by ₹300.00; its rate carries a margin of 5.25 paise per dollar against Bank A's 6 paise

self_check.prompt_text: For an importer buying dollars, which side of the interbank quote do you compare a bank's all-in rate with, and what does the difference tell you?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The interbank selling (offer) rate, because the bank is selling. The excess of the all-in rate over that rate is the margin the bank is charging.

items.stem_md: A bank's dealer quotes USD/INR 83.2450/83.2550 (illustrative rates). A garment exporter sells USD 20,000 to this bank at the quoted rate, with no further margin. Which rate applies, and why?

options.text_md: 83.2550, because the exporter is the seller and a seller gets the offer
options.explanation_md: Bid and offer are named from the quoting bank's side. The offer is where the bank sells, not where the customer sells.

options.text_md: 83.2450, because the bank is buying dollars and it buys at its bid
options.explanation_md: The exporter's sale is the bank's purchase, and the quoting bank buys at the lower, bid side of a direct quote.

options.text_md: 83.2500, because a customer deal is done at the midpoint of the quote
options.explanation_md: The midpoint is not a dealing rate. The bank deals at its bid or its offer.

options.text_md: 83.2400, because a customer always deals a little below the quoted bid
options.explanation_md: Nothing is deducted here: the question says the deal is done at the quoted rate with no further margin.

items.correct_explanation_md: Look at the deal from the quoting bank's side: it is buying dollars. In a direct quote the bank buys at the first, lower rate (the bid), so the exporter receives ₹83.2450 per dollar.

items.stem_md: Two banks strike a USD/INR deal on Thursday, 12 November 2026 for value **spot**. Saturday and Sunday are not working days, and there are no other holidays in either centre. On which date do the funds settle?

options.text_md: Friday, 13 November 2026
options.explanation_md: The next working day after the deal date is value tom, not spot.

options.text_md: Saturday, 14 November 2026
options.explanation_md: This counts two calendar days. Spot counts working days, and Saturday is not one.

options.text_md: Monday, 16 November 2026
options.explanation_md: Friday is the first working day after the deal; the weekend is skipped, so Monday is the second.

options.text_md: Tuesday, 17 November 2026
options.explanation_md: This is the third working day after the deal. A date after the spot date would make it a forward.

items.correct_explanation_md: Spot settles on the second working day after the deal date. From Thursday, Friday is the first working day; Saturday and Sunday do not count and push settlement on; Monday, 16 November 2026 is the second.

items.stem_md: A customer's account was debited ₹10,43,718.75 for an outward remittance of USD 12,500, before charges and taxes. At that moment interbank spot USD/INR was 83.4125/83.4175 (illustrative rates). How much exchange margin, in paise per dollar, did the bank load on the deal?

items.correct_explanation_md: First find the rate the customer actually paid: 10,43,718.75 ÷ 12,500 = 83.4975. An outward remittance is a sale of dollars by the bank, so compare with the interbank selling rate: 83.4975 − 83.4175 = 0.0800 rupees, which is 8 paise per dollar. Comparing with the buying rate (83.4125) would overstate the margin as 8.5 paise.

worked_solution_steps.description: The bank sold dollars, so the base is the interbank selling rate.
Margin is the excess over that rate, converted to paise.

items.title: Who is in the forex market, and what each is there for
items.core_explanation_md:
The foreign exchange market has no building. It is a web of dealing rooms and screens that passes business from centre to centre round the clock, Monday to Friday: Tokyo and Sydney first, then Singapore, India and the Gulf, then Frankfurt and London, and New York last. Most deals are struck over the counter, by phone or on electronic platforms.

Three kinds of player meet there:

- **The steerer.** A central bank manages the country's reserves and steps in to calm swings in its own currency.
- **The price makers and go-betweens.** Large commercial banks quote a buying and a selling rate at the same time, deal for customers and for their own books, and take views on rates. Brokers act as middlemen between the others.
- **The users.** Investment funds, companies and individuals come for a reason outside the market: investing abroad, hedging, paying for trade, travel.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Why does it matter who is on the other side? Because the motive tells you how to read the move. A bank that quotes both sides all day gives the market its depth: a caller can deal either way at once. A central bank dealing in size is usually not chasing a profit; it is smoothing the value of the home currency.

items.title: Forward rate from spot rate and forward margin
items.core_explanation_md:
A forward rate is built, not guessed: take today's spot rate and adjust it by the forward margin for the period. If the foreign currency costs more for future delivery than for spot, it is at a **premium** and the margin is added. If it costs less, it is at a **discount** and the margin is subtracted.

The two currencies of a pair always mirror each other: when the dollar is at a premium against the rupee, the rupee is at a discount against the dollar.
items.expanded_explanation_md: What sets the margin? Mainly the gap between interest rates in the two currencies, together with expected demand and supply for them. So a forward rate is an expectation written into today's prices. It is not a promise about where the spot rate will stand on that date.

variables.name: Forward rate
variables.unit: home currency per unit of foreign currency

variables.name: Spot rate
variables.unit: home currency per unit of foreign currency

variables.name: Forward margin: positive for a premium, negative for a discount

assumptions: Direct quotation: home currency per unit of foreign currency.
The spot rate and the margin are for the same side of the quote, buying or selling.
The margin is for the same period as the forward contract.
common_errors: Adding a discount instead of subtracting it.
Adding a margin quoted in paise or pips to a rate in rupees without converting it first.
Forgetting that a premium on one currency of the pair is a discount on the other.

self_check.expected_takeaway: 83.10: the discount is subtracted, 83.40 − 0.30. With the dollar at a discount, the rupee is at a premium.

items.title: No EUR/INR quote on the screen: an exporter's rate by the chain rule
items.core_explanation_md: In India a straight interbank quote exists for USD/INR; other currencies reach the rupee through the dollar. Illustrative case: a Coimbatore textile exporter receives EUR 25,000. The dealer sees EUR/USD 1.0836/1.0841 and USD/INR 83.4125/83.4175. What interbank EUR/INR rate does the bank start from, before its own margin?

worked_steps.description: Follow the money. The bank buys euros from the exporter, so to square itself it sells those euros for dollars: the market buys euros at its bid.
It then sells the dollars for rupees: the market buys dollars at its bid.
Chain the two so that the dollar cancels.
Rupees for the exporter at that rate, before the bank's margin.

items.final_answer_with_unit: Interbank EUR/INR buying rate ₹90.3858 per EUR; EUR 25,000 is worth ₹22,59,645.00 before margin

self_check.prompt_text: For the exporter's euros, why are both legs taken at the bid, and what would change for an importer who needs euros?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The bank is selling in both legs (euros for dollars, then dollars for rupees), and the market buys at its bid each time. For an importer the bank buys in both legs, so both legs are taken at the offer.

items.stem_md: The rupee swings sharply within an hour of trading. One participant sells dollars from the country's reserves, not to earn a profit but to steady the rate. Which participant is acting in its expected role?

options.text_md: A forex broker matching a buyer with a seller

options.explanation_md: A central bank manages the reserves and uses the market to reduce volatility in the value of the home currency.

options.text_md: A company covering an import payment
options.explanation_md: A company comes to the market for its own trade or investment needs, not to steady the exchange rate.

items.title: Value dates: when the money actually moves
items.core_explanation_md:
Agreeing a rate and exchanging the money are two different moments. The day the currencies really change hands is the **value date**, and its name tells you how far it is from the deal date:

| Name | Money moves |
| --- | --- |
| Cash (ready) | the same day |
| Tom | the next working day |
| Spot | the second working day |
| Forward | any day after spot |

Spot is the market's normal basis, and other rates for a currency are built from the spot rate. Count **working** days: a Saturday, Sunday or holiday in a centre where the currency is settled pushes the date to the next working day.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Why two days for spot? Deals are struck across time zones, and both banks need time to instruct payment in two different countries. A deal done for an earlier date than spot (cash or tom) or a later one (forward) is priced by adjusting the spot rate.

self_check.prompt_text: Without looking: name the four value dates in order and say what happens when the date falls on a weekend.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Cash (same day), tom (next working day), spot (second working day), forward (any later day). A weekend or holiday moves settlement to the next working day.

items.title: What moves an exchange rate: slow forces, frictions and expectations
items.core_explanation_md:
Three kinds of pressure act on a currency, and they work on different clocks.

- **Fundamentals** are the slow forces that come from the economy and its policies: the balance of payments (a surplus tends to strengthen the home currency, a deficit to weaken it), growth, fiscal and monetary policy, interest rates and political stability. They shape the rate over the long run.
- **Technical reasons** are frictions in how money is allowed to move: government controls that hold a currency at an unrealistic value, and freedom or restriction on capital flows. Capital tends to move from lower-yielding to higher-yielding currencies.
- **Speculation** is expectation turned into deals: if a fall is expected, players buy the foreign currency now, and the belief can spread and move the rate by itself.
items.expanded_explanation_md:
Interest rates cut both ways. A rise in domestic rates tends to pull in overseas capital, so the currency firms up in the short term. Kept high for long, the same rates slow the economy, and that weakens the currency over time.

Speculation is not only a threat: speculative deals also add depth and liquidity to the market.

items.title: Book the dollars forward, or wait? An importer's break-even
items.core_explanation_md: A customer's forward rate is built in the same way as a spot customer rate, with one more layer: the forward margin. Illustrative case: an importer must pay USD 50,000 in three months. Interbank spot USD/INR is 83.4125/83.4175, the dollar's three-month premium on the selling side is 42 paise, and the bank's exchange margin is 5 paise. What rate fixes the cost today, and how high must the dollar go for the forward to have been the cheaper choice?

worked_steps.description: The bank will sell dollars, so start from the interbank selling rate.
Add the full three-month premium to reach the interbank forward rate.
Add the exchange margin, because the bank sells high.
Cost fixed by the forward contract.
Break-even: with the same 5 paise margin on a spot purchase in three months, waiting costs the same when the interbank selling rate then equals the forward interbank rate.

items.final_answer_with_unit: Forward rate ₹83.8875 per USD, fixing the cost at ₹41,94,375.00; waiting is dearer only if the interbank selling rate in three months is above 83.8375

self_check.prompt_text: List, in order, the three figures added together to get an importer's forward rate.
self_check.expected_takeaway: The interbank spot selling rate, the forward premium for the period, and the bank's exchange margin.

items.stem_md: A country raises its domestic interest rates sharply and keeps them high for several years. Going by the fundamental factors, what is the expected effect on its currency?

options.text_md: It firms up in the short term as overseas capital comes in, then tends to weaken as high rates slow the economy
options.explanation_md: High rates attract capital at first; kept high, they slow the economy, which weakens the currency over the longer term.

options.text_md: It weakens at once and keeps weakening, because high rates always mean a weak currency
options.explanation_md: The first effect of higher rates is the opposite: they tend to draw in overseas capital.

options.text_md: It strengthens in the short term and keeps strengthening for as long as rates stay high
options.explanation_md: The short-term part is right, but over the longer term high rates slow the economy and weaken the currency.

options.text_md: Nothing changes, because interest rates are a technical factor that affects only forward margins
options.explanation_md: Interest rates are listed among the fundamental reasons and do act on the exchange rate.

items.correct_explanation_md: Interest rates work in two stages. Higher domestic rates tend to attract overseas capital, so the currency appreciates in the short term. Over the longer term, high rates slow the economy down and that weakens the home currency.

items.stem_md: For years a government holds its currency at a fixed level through exchange controls. When the controls are lifted, the rate moves violently within days. Which kind of reason best explains the movement?

options.text_md: A technical reason, because controls had kept the currency at an unrealistic value
options.explanation_md: Government controls and restrictions on capital movement are technical reasons, and they can end in violent rate movements.

options.text_md: Speculation, because any sharp movement is caused by speculators
options.explanation_md: Speculation can move rates, but the case describes controls holding an unrealistic value, not deals driven by expectation.

options.text_md: A fundamental reason, because political stability has improved
options.explanation_md: The case gives no information about political stability.

items.correct_explanation_md: Government controls that hold a currency at an unrealistic value, and the freedom or restriction of capital movement, are technical reasons. When such controls go, the rate can move violently towards a realistic level.

items.title: Who deals, who watches, who settles
items.core_explanation_md:
A bank's foreign exchange dealing room does more than trade. It serves customers and other branches, manages the bank's foreign currency assets and liabilities and its Nostro accounts, and can also take positions for profit.

The one rule that holds the arrangement together is **separation of duties**. Three functions are kept apart:

- **Front office**: the dealers who quote and deal.
- **Mid office**: measures and watches the risk the dealers take, supplies market information, and helps ensure compliance. It stands independent of the dealers.
- **Back office**: confirms and settles deals, does the accounting and reconciles accounts. It both supports the dealers and checks them.

No single person should be able to deal, record and settle the same transaction. That is what stops a mistake, or a worse act, from going unseen.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Ask of any task: is it taking the risk, measuring the risk, or recording what happened? Dealing is the first, risk monitoring and limit checks the second, and confirmation, settlement and reconciliation the third. A lax back office can cancel the dealers' profits or let wrongdoing pass unnoticed, which is why it is given a checking role and not only a clerical one.

items.title: Five ways a dealing room can lose money
items.core_explanation_md:
Managing a dealing room means knowing what can go wrong. Five risks matter:

- **Operational**: people, systems or procedures fail: an error, a breakdown, a missing control.
- **Exchange**: rates move, or receivables and payables in a currency do not match.
- **Credit**: the other side cannot or will not perform. Two stages: *before maturity* (you must replace the deal at today's market rates with a new counterparty) and *during settlement* (one side has paid and the other has not).
- **Liquidity**: liabilities fall due faster than assets can be turned into cash, because maturities do not match.
- **Market**: rates or prices move against you and you cannot get out in time. It shows up as interest rate, equity price and currency risk.

The board of a bank is expected to set a policy and limits for dealing; the five risks are what those limits are meant to contain.

self_check.prompt_text: A counterparty fails while a deal is still open and before any money has moved. Which of the five risks has arisen, and what does the bank now have to do?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Credit risk, at the pre-settlement stage: the bank must cover the transaction at current market rates with a new counterparty.

items.title: Settlement risk against pre-settlement risk: the same deal, two failures
items.core_explanation_md: The two stages of credit risk can differ enormously in size. Illustrative case: a Frankfurt bank sells EUR 800,000 to a New York bank at EUR/USD 1.0840, value spot. The euros are paid in Frankfurt in the morning; the dollars are due only when New York opens hours later. Compare (a) the New York bank failing **after** the euros are paid but before it pays the dollars, with (b) it failing **before** settlement, when the market has moved to EUR/USD 1.0790.

worked_steps.description: Dollars the Frankfurt bank is owed under the deal.
Case (a), settlement risk: the euros have gone and nothing has come back. The bank's whole claim is at risk.
Case (b), pre-settlement risk: nothing has been paid, so the bank only has to re-do the sale at today's rate. Dollars it would now receive.
Loss from having to re-do the sale at the worse rate.

items.final_answer_with_unit: Settlement risk puts USD 867,200.00 at stake; pre-settlement risk costs only USD 4,000.00 (the rate move)

self_check.prompt_text: Why is the loss so much smaller when the counterparty fails before settlement?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Nothing has been paid yet, so the loss is only the cost of replacing the deal at the new market rate, not the whole principal.

items.stem_md: In a bank's foreign exchange operations, which part of the organisation confirms the deals, settles them and reconciles the accounts?

options.text_md: The front office, because the dealers know the terms best
options.explanation_md: Dealers take the risk. Letting them also settle and record their own deals would remove the separation of duties.

options.text_md: The mid office, because it watches the risk the dealers take
options.explanation_md: The mid office measures and monitors risk and supports compliance; it does not settle or reconcile.

options.text_md: The back office, which also acts as a check on the dealers
options.explanation_md: Confirmation, settlement, accounting and reconciliation are the back office's work, and it checks as well as supports the dealers.

options.text_md: The head dealer, who signs off every deal at day end
options.explanation_md: A dealer, even a senior one, belongs to the front office; keeping settlement separate from dealing is the point.

items.correct_explanation_md: The back office confirms and settles deals, keeps the accounts and reconciles them, and by doing so also checks the dealers. Dealing (front office) and risk monitoring (mid office) are deliberately kept separate from it.

items.stem_md: A bank in Frankfurt pays out the euro leg of a spot deal in the morning. The New York counterparty is due to pay the dollar leg after its market opens, and fails before doing so. Which risk has caused the loss?

options.text_md: Pre-settlement risk, because the counterparty failed before the deal was complete
options.explanation_md: Pre-settlement risk is failure before any settlement begins, where the loss is the cost of replacing the deal. Here one leg has already been paid.

options.text_md: Settlement risk, arising from the time-zone gap between the two payments
options.explanation_md: One party delivered its currency and the other failed before delivering its own, because the payments fall in different time zones.

options.text_md: Interest rate risk, because the dollar payment was delayed
options.explanation_md: Interest rate risk is the effect of rate changes on the bank's assets and liabilities; it is not a failure to pay.

options.text_md: Equity price risk, because the loss arose on a market in New York
options.explanation_md: Equity price risk concerns the price of shares held; nothing in the case involves shares.

items.correct_explanation_md: The Frankfurt bank has delivered its euros and the counterparty has failed before delivering dollars, with the time-zone difference between the two payments creating the gap. That is settlement risk, the kind the 1974 Herstatt failure made famous.

items.stem_md: A bank bought USD 500,000 forward from a counterparty at 83.9000 (illustrative figures). Before the maturity date, with nothing yet paid, the counterparty fails. The bank covers by buying USD 500,000 for the same maturity from a new counterparty at 84.1250. What extra cost, in rupees, does the bank bear because of the failure?

numeric_rule.rounding_instruction: Give the amount to 2 decimal places.

items.correct_explanation_md: Before maturity and before any payment, the loss from a counterparty's failure is the cost of replacing the deal at the ongoing market rate. The dollars now cost 84.1250 instead of 83.9000, so the extra cost is 500,000 × (84.1250 − 83.9000) = 500,000 × 0.2250 = ₹1,12,500.00. The full value of the contract (about ₹4.2 crore) was never at risk, because nothing had been paid.

worked_solution_steps.description: Extra rupees per dollar to replace the contract.
Multiply by the dollars to be replaced.

items.title: Forward or future: who writes the terms, and who stands behind the deal
items.core_explanation_md:
A derivative is a product whose value is derived from something else, such as a currency position. Used to take a view it is speculation; used to cut the risk in everyday cash flows it is hedging.

Two derivatives fix a future exchange rate today, and they differ on two questions.

- **Who writes the terms?** A **forward** is negotiated between a customer and a bank, in any size and for the dates they agree. A **future** is a standard contract, in a fixed size, traded on an exchange.
- **Who stands behind it?** In a forward you rely on the other party, and no collateral is demanded explicitly. In a future the clearing house sits between buyer and seller and guarantees both, and it protects itself by collecting margins.

A forward is typically settled by delivery or cancellation on the due date. A future is usually closed out by taking an opposite position.
items.expanded_explanation_md: That is why a forward is the usual tool for an exporter or importer with a known amount and date: it can be tailored. The standard future suits those who want a traded, guaranteed contract and can manage margin calls.

items.title: Options: a right you pay for
items.core_explanation_md:
An option gives its buyer the **right, not the obligation**, to buy or sell currency at a fixed price during a set period. Because the buyer can walk away, the buyer pays for the right: the **premium**.

- A **call** is a right to buy; a **put** is a right to sell. In currency business calls tend to suit importers and puts exporters.
- The buyer is the **holder**; the seller is the **writer** (or grantor).
- The fixed price is the **strike** (exercise) price.
- An **American** option can be exercised at any time up to expiry; a **European** option only on the expiry date.

Compare the strike with today's spot rate, ignoring the premium: if exercising now would pay, the option is **in the money**; if not, **out of the money**; if strike and spot are equal, **at the money**.

self_check.prompt_text: An importer holds a call on dollars with a strike of 84.00. Spot is 84.50. Is the option in, at or out of the money, and why?
self_check.expected_takeaway: In the money: exercising lets the importer buy at 84.00 what costs 84.50 in the market, a gain before the premium.

items.title: An importer's call option: the cost in two futures
items.core_explanation_md: Illustrative case: an importer must buy USD 100,000 in three months and does not want to pay more than about ₹84.35 per dollar. It buys a call option with a strike of ₹84.00 and pays a premium of ₹0.35 per dollar at the start. Work out the effective cost per dollar and the total outlay if, at expiry, spot is (a) 84.80 or (b) 83.60. Ignore interest on the premium.

worked_steps.description: Premium paid on day one for USD 100,000.
Case (a), spot 84.80: the call is in the money (strike 84.00 is below spot). Exercise it and buy at the strike.
Total outlay in case (a): strike cost plus premium.
Case (b), spot 83.60: the call is out of the money. Let it lapse and buy in the market.
Total outlay in case (b): market cost plus the premium already paid.

items.final_answer_with_unit: Outlay ₹84,35,000.00 (₹84.35 per USD) if spot is 84.80; ₹83,95,000.00 (₹83.95 per USD) if spot is 83.60. The importer's cost is capped at ₹84.35 per USD and it still gains if the rupee strengthens

self_check.prompt_text: What does the premium buy the importer, and what is the most the importer can end up paying per dollar here?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The right to buy at the strike whatever happens to spot, and so a cap on the cost: strike plus premium, ₹84.35 per dollar.

items.stem_md: A corporate wants a currency contract in which the credit risk of the other side is taken over by a clearing house, which collects margins to protect itself. Which contract fits?

options.text_md: A forward contract with its bank, because the bank guarantees delivery
options.explanation_md: A forward is between the customer and the bank, which is the counterparty; no clearing house stands between them.

options.text_md: A foreign currency futures contract traded on an exchange
options.explanation_md: In an exchange-traded futures contract the clearing house guarantees both sides and manages credit risk through margins.

options.text_md: A tailor-made over-the-counter swap agreed privately with a dealer
options.explanation_md: A privately agreed swap is a contract between two parties; no clearing house is involved.

options.text_md: A spot deal, because settlement is two working days away
options.explanation_md: A spot deal is not a derivative, and the nature of the counterparty's risk is not changed by settlement timing.

items.correct_explanation_md: Futures are standardised and traded on an exchange, where the clearing house conducts the trade and guarantees both buyer and seller, managing credit risk through margins. A forward relies on the counterparty.

items.stem_md: A company pays a fixed rate of 7.10% p.a. and receives a floating rate on an interest rate swap with a notional amount of ₹20,00,00,000 (illustrative figures). For one quarter the floating rate is 6.90% p.a. Treat a quarter as exactly one-quarter of a year, and assume cash flows are netted and no principal is exchanged. What net amount does the company pay for the quarter, in rupees?

numeric_rule.rounding_instruction: Give the amount to 2 decimal places.

items.correct_explanation_md: Both interest flows are worked on the notional amount, which is never itself exchanged. Fixed leg for the quarter: 20,00,00,000 × 7.10% ÷ 4 = ₹35,50,000. Floating leg: 20,00,00,000 × 6.90% ÷ 4 = ₹34,50,000. The company pays the larger and receives the smaller, so the net payment is ₹1,00,000.

worked_solution_steps.description: Net payment by the fixed-rate payer.

items.stem_md: An exporter holds a put option on US dollars with a strike of ₹83.00. Spot USD/INR is now ₹84.00. Ignoring the premium, how is the option described?

options.text_md: In the money, because the strike is below the spot rate
options.explanation_md: That reasoning suits a call. A put is a right to sell: the exporter would sell at 83.00 what the market pays 84.00 for.

options.text_md: At the money, because the strike and spot are within one rupee
options.explanation_md: At the money means the strike equals the spot rate; being close is not enough.

options.text_md: Out of the money, because selling at the strike would give less than the market
options.explanation_md: Exercising now would not be profitable, since the exporter would receive 83.00 instead of selling at 84.00 in the market.

options.text_md: Out of the money, because a put can only be exercised on the expiry date
options.explanation_md: Whether a put can be exercised early depends on whether it is American or European; that is not what decides how far in or out of the money it is.

items.correct_explanation_md: A put is the right to sell at the strike. With a strike of 83.00 and spot at 84.00, exercising would earn less than the market pays, so exercising now would not be profitable: the option is out of the money.
